passages.where: The psalm says God is our refuge and strength, so we will not fear though the earth gives way and the mountains fall into the sea. The site's plain note says it does not tell you not to fear because nothing bad will happen; it tells you not to fear because of who is with you when it does. The psalm puts God next to the trouble without making the trouble small.

As Assyria threatens and the people of Judah panic, God tells Isaiah not to call conspiracy everything the people call conspiracy, and not to fear what they fear: the LORD of Hosts is the one to regard as holy and to fear. The site's note on the chapter says Isaiah is told to fear the Lord, who will be a sanctuary for some. A people's shared dread is not a reliable guide to what is true.

Some in the crowd bring Jesus the news of Galileans killed by Pilate. The site's note says Jesus names the assumption behind the report before anyone voices it, that the victims must have been worse sinners, and denies it flatly. The plain note says he turns the question from what the dead had done to where the living stand with God. It shows how to hear bad news: without blaming the victims, and without imagining we are safer than they were.

On the night before his death Jesus tells his disciples that in the world they will have tribulation, but to take courage, because he has overcome the world. The site's plain note says he does not deny the trouble; he says it does not have the last word. The victory is real now, and it is not yet complete.

The proverb observes that the first to state his case seems right until another comes and examines him. The site's note on the chapter gathers its sayings on hasty answers and lawsuits. A first report, however confident, is not yet the whole story, and wisdom waits for the other side.

Jeremiah writes to exiles in Babylon in 597 BC, telling them to build houses, plant gardens, raise families and pray for the welfare of the city where they live. The site's note says he warned against prophets promising a quick return. In a world that was not theirs and was not getting better on their schedule, God's people were told to seek its good.

Facing a king's order to kill all the wise men, Daniel and his friends pray, and when God reveals the mystery Daniel blesses him: he changes times and seasons, removes kings and establishes them. The site's note tells how the dream ended in a stone that became a mountain filling the earth. Rulers rise and fall in every age; the one who sets them up does not.

The psalm asks why the nations rage and the rulers plot, and answers that the One enthroned in heaven laughs. The site's note says the contrast in posture is the argument: the rebels stand, God sits. The plain note adds that the first Christians prayed this psalm not for revenge, but for courage.

Among Paul's short commands about sincere love is this one: rejoice with those who rejoice; weep with those who weep. The news brings a stream of other people's sorrow. Scripture's answer is neither to look away nor to be swallowed by dread, but to weep with real people and pray for them.

Habakkuk, trembling at what is coming, says that though the fig tree does not bud and the fields produce no food, yet he will rejoice in the God of his salvation. The site's note says he resolves to wait quietly for the day of distress. His joy did not depend on the headlines of his own day.

misread.taken: Wars and rumors of wars are read in the news as proof that the end is about to come, so that every new war, earthquake or crisis is treated as a countdown and a reason for fear.
misread.says: The site's plain note says every age has had wars, earthquakes and famines, and in every age someone has said they prove the end is here. Jesus says the opposite: these things must happen, but the end is still to come. They are not a countdown; they are the normal weather of a broken world, and Jesus tells his followers not to be alarmed. The note adds that the first danger Jesus names is not war but being fooled, and asks who we let tell us what the news means.

whole: For many people bad news now arrives all day long. A war on the other side of the world, a shooting, a storm, an election, a scandal, a market falling: it arrives on the phone before breakfast and follows them to bed. Some of it is close and real; much of it is far away and out of their hands. They feel they ought to know, and they feel worse for knowing. Some find themselves anxious, some angry, some numb, and many sure that everything is falling apart and that the other side is to blame. The feeling of dread can grow quite apart from anything in their own street or week.

Scripture knew rumors and panic long before screens. Isaiah's neighbors saw conspiracy everywhere as Assyria marched, and God told him not to fear what they feared. A crowd brought Jesus the news of Galileans killed by Pilate and assumed the victims must have deserved it. Jesus warned that people would point to every war and earthquake as a sign, and that the first danger was being fooled. Our own fear often has a shape the Bible recognizes: we let the loudest voice tell us what is happening and what it means, we look for someone to blame so that we can feel safer, and we treat the news as if it decided everything. That temptation runs in every direction, through every party and every church, and it runs through us.

So the Bible's wisdom is to fear God and not the crowd, and to love the people the news is about. Listen to the second witness before you decide, as Proverbs says. Refuse to blame the victims of disaster, as Jesus refused. Weep with those who weep and pray for them by name. Seek the good of the place where you live, as the exiles in Babylon were told to do, rather than only fearing what may become of it. It may mean choosing when and how much news to take in, and putting the phone down before sleep. It means turning from what the headlines say to who God is, the one who changes times and seasons and sets up rulers and removes them.

The hope Scripture gives is that history is not running loose. God is our refuge and strength, an ever-present help in times of trouble, and the One enthroned in heaven is not anxious. In the world there will be tribulation, Jesus said, but take courage: he has overcome the world. The kingdom Daniel saw grows like a stone into a mountain, slowly and surely, while kingdoms rise and fall around it. Bad news will keep coming until he comes. It does not get to decide who we are, or what we hope in.
sit: Who or what has been telling you what the news means, and what would change if you prayed for the people in the next headline instead of only fearing it?

prayer.lead: The end of the psalm of the toppling mountains, where God's own voice says be still and know that I am God. The site's plain note on the psalm says it does not make the trouble small; it puts God next to it.
